result:
The first thing I learned at the town's lost property office was never to shake an umbrella indoors. The second was that a person who has lost an umbrella cannot remember its color, but can describe with perfect accuracy the sound it makes when opened. “Like someone sitting on a biscuit tin,” said a woman on my first morning. We had thirty umbrellas. I opened six before she nodded. Outside, the sun was shining. She carried her umbrella home under her arm with the grave satisfaction of a musician who has just got a difficult instrument back in tune.

My job was supposed to last a summer. I was nineteen, saving for a room in a city where nobody would know which primary school I had attended. The office occupied the old station buffet. Behind my desk, a tiled sign still offered TEA AND A SLICE for a price no longer possible in any currency. Trains stopped there four times a day. Between them, I accessioned scarves, spectacles, shopping bags, single gloves, and an alarming number of dentures. My supervisor, Len, insisted that dentures be recorded as “one set, partial” rather than “several teeth.” He had standards.

In July somebody handed in a door. It was narrow and blue, with a brass hook on one side and a penciled ladder of children's heights on the other. The finder had seen it lying beside the bicycle racks. Len and I stood it against the wall. Neither of us could imagine how to lose a door. You might forget that you had brought your gloves; surely you would remember walking down the street behind a broad sheet of wood, unable to see anything except your shoes and the occasional terrified pigeon escaping from underneath.

The local paper ran a photograph. For scale, the photographer asked me to stand beside the door, which made me look like a contestant on a quiz show with exceptionally poor prizes. Within days we had visitors. A carpenter identified the wood as pine. A retired teacher recognized the handwriting beside the height marks, then put on her glasses and withdrew her claim. Two little boys asked permission to measure themselves. Soon there were fresh pencil lines labeled Robin and Tim, and I had technically violated the rule against altering an article in custody.

Len pretended not to notice. He had begun eating his sandwiches beside the door, sitting on an upturned crate, reading yesterday's racing results. One afternoon I found him with his thumbnail resting on a notch halfway up the frame. “My sister used to cheat,” he said. “She'd draw herself taller after we'd gone to bed.” I asked whether his parents had minded. “Minded? They thought she'd developed a remarkable capacity to grow on Thursdays.” He finished his sandwich. It contained cucumber sliced almost transparent, the way his wife had liked it. She had died in February.

By August the door had acquired a reputation quite independent of its owner. People brought visiting cousins to see it. A girl with a red fringe made a careful drawing of its hinges. Someone left a pot of geraniums at its foot, as if the rest of the house might materialize if properly encouraged. I started to dread the arrival of anyone who looked purposeful. I liked our office better with the door in it. This struck me as an unprofessional feeling, particularly since the whole point of the office was to give everything back.

Its owner arrived on a wet Tuesday, wheeling a bicycle with one pedal missing. She was about forty, in painty trousers, and she laughed when she saw the geraniums. The door had come from her father's pantry. She had been taking it to the tip on a borrowed trailer when the strap worked loose. By the time she noticed, she was three miles away and late for a dental appointment. “I thought, well, somebody'll make use of it,” she said. “I didn't expect quite this.” She touched the line labeled Tim. “He's tall for seven.”

I fetched the release form. Under distinguishing features, she wrote a small burn behind the hook. We checked. There it was, a brown crescent, caused by her brother trying to dry a sock with a candle in 1978. He had blamed their mother for buying flammable socks. Len laughed so hard he had to take off his glasses. The woman signed, folded her copy into a pocket, and regarded the door with some dismay. We regarded her bicycle. The afternoon train came and went. Rain rattled against the glass roof over the empty platform.

In the end she took only the brass hook. Len found a screwdriver, and she held out her hand for the screws, two dull little things that had spent half a century in the dark. She said she would put the hook beside her kitchen sink for tea towels. The door stayed. When the office closed three years later, it became a tabletop in the station café. I know because I went back last April and ate a buttered bun with my elbows resting somewhere between Robin and Tim.

I live in the city now. Last week I put a hook beside my own sink, a cheap one from the hardware shop, fixed slightly crooked because the drill met something stubborn in the wall. My daughter hangs her apron there. This morning I caught her standing on a chair, trying to get it down without asking for help. I nearly told her she had grown. Instead I fetched a pencil and stood her against the pantry door. She insisted on keeping her shoes on. After some negotiation, we wrote that detail down too. One day somebody looking at that mark will want to know whether the half inch belonged to the child or to the shoes. I see no reason to leave the matter to chance.
